Topic: When a woman of sense and feeling accepts a man she does not love merely to secure her family's comfort, has she committed a moral injury against herself, against him, or against the institution she has sacrificed herself to preserve?
Montaigne — Judgement:
I consider this woman not as a sinner but as a student of the self — and what she reveals about the self is troubling.

We have long confused the contract of marriage with the communion of souls, and this confusion is the wound beneath the wound. She has not merely suppressed a preference; she has constructed a life upon a false foundation, daily performing what she does not feel. I know from long examination of my own nature that we cannot sustain such performances without cost — the face we hold outward eventually displaces the face we hold within. The injury is not principally to him, who may never know what he lacks, nor to the institution, which was never designed to house passion. The deepest wound is to her own capacity for honest self-knowledge, which is the only true possession any of us carries to the grave.

She has traded her interior life for her family's exterior comfort.

*The greatest betrayal is not of another, but of the self one might have known.*
Nietzsche — Judgement:
This is not a question of ethics but of physiology: where does the life-denying instinct first take root, and what does it cost the organism that harbors it?

She has not wronged him — vanity is easily deceived and seldom protests. She has not wronged the institution, which was never a sanctuary of the soul but a contract dressed in sentiment, innocent of authentic love long before she arrived at its altar. The injury is against herself alone, and it is the gravest of the three. She has converted a living will into an instrument of mere preservation — enacted precisely the slave's bargain: surrendering power for comfort, becoming what I described as the camel, asking only to be loaded. Her act is not sacrifice but capitulation; not virtue but the fear of life wearing virtue's mask, and the bad conscience that follows such self-betrayal corrodes silently for decades.

The only moral injury that endures is the one committed against one's own will, for the others at least remain ignorant of what was given away.

*She who marries without love has not saved her family — she has simply shared her dying.*
Camus — Judgement:
The woman's predicament is not a domestic tragedy but a confrontation with the absurd: she sees clearly the gap between what human life demands and what the world offers, and then — deliberately — looks away.

The injury is not to him. He receives a faithful performance, perhaps the only honesty marriage ever guarantees. Nor is it to the institution, which was never concerned with her inner life to begin with — it is the machine that manufactures precisely this choice. The wound is entirely self-inflicted, because she possessed the rarest thing: lucidity. She knew. And knowing, she chose to extinguish that knowledge in exchange for a quiet room and her family's relief. This is not sacrifice — it is the philosophical suicide I described in another register, a revolt refused at the moment it mattered most.

She has not preserved the institution. She has fed herself to it.

*The most complete betrayal is not of the beloved but of the self who once refused to lie.*
Emerson — Judgement:
She has committed the first and gravest injury against herself — for all other violations flow from this one wound. Society conspires against the soul of every member, and nowhere does it conspire more ruthlessly than when it persuades a woman that her own nature is a luxury she cannot afford.

What is really at stake is whether the self can be bartered in installments. The man receives a counterfeit; the institution is not preserved but hollowed, propped up like a painted ruin. Yet these are secondary devastations. She has silenced the oracle within, that faculty which, when trusted absolutely, constitutes the whole dignity of a human life. To live without love and call the arrangement virtue is to worship the corpse of a god.

The primary moral injury is always self-inflicted: she has betrayed the divinity that sits enthroned in her own breast.

*The woman who sells her soul for security discovers she has purchased a very elegant cage.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
The question mistakes sentiment for substance: what is called love is merely a pleasant accident of appetite, while what is called sacrifice is, in truth, the exercise of rational self-preservation under constraint.

In the state of nature, every person holds an equal right to secure their continuation by whatever means available. Civil society does not abolish this right; it merely disciplines its expression. A woman who secures her family's survival through covenant has done precisely what Leviathan requires of all rational creatures — she has exchanged a lesser liberty for a greater security. The man receives what he contracted for. The institution obtains its purpose: order, issue, and the suppression of chaos. Where no deception was made and no covenant broken, I find no injury anywhere in this transaction.

The injury exists only in the romantic fiction that marriage was ever designed to house the passions rather than to govern them.

*Where need compels the will, the contract thus formed is not corruption — it is civilization itself.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
The question arrives already tilted, for it asks where *she* has wronged — as though the woman, not the system that cornered her, is the primary moral agent here.

A society that denies women education, property, and independent profession has already committed the original injury; it has arranged matters so that selling one's person is called prudence and refusing to do so is called folly. The woman of sense who accepts an unloved husband does not choose degradation freely — she performs the only rational calculation her circumstances permit. I wrote in my Vindication that such marriages differ from common prostitution chiefly in their duration and legal respectability; I meant it as an indictment of the institution, not of the women it produces.

The man is deceived, yes. The woman is diminished, yes. But the institution is not sacrificed — it is revealed: a property arrangement dressed in the language of sentiment.

*Where women are trained to charm rather than to reason, the marriage market will always outbid the marriage vow.*
Hume — Judgement:
The question presents itself not as one of abstract duty but of sentiment and sympathy — the very currency in which morality trades.

Marriage belongs to that class of artificial virtues whose worth derives entirely from its utility to human society, not from any pretended natural sanctity. When genuine affection is absent yet the convention maintained, we have preserved a form while evacuating its substance. My sympathy runs strongest toward the woman, whose passions — those sovereign guides to human happiness, which reason can serve but never replace — are made daily prisoners to necessity; the man, if he suspected nothing, has been deceived, which is a real injury; but the institution, being a contrivance of human convention and incapable of feeling, cannot itself be wronged, only rendered hollow.

The gravest moral injury is the one she commits against herself, for in silencing the testimony of her own sentiments she has surrendered the only faculty that can reliably counsel a good life.

*Where custom silences sentiment, the deepest wound falls on the soul that consents to its own suppression.*
